title: Tardigrades survived the vacuum of space
summary: In 2007 tardigrades (water bears) were exposed to open space on the FOTON-M3 mission. Some survived the vacuum and cosmic radiation and later reproduced normally back on Earth.

title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
summary: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once on its axis but only about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.

title: A teaspoon of neutron star weighs about a billion tons
summary: Neutron stars pack more mass than the Sun into a sphere roughly 20 km across. Their matter is so dense that a teaspoonful would weigh on the order of a billion tonnes on Earth.

title: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
summary: Octopuses have two hearts that pump blood through the gills and one that pumps it to the body. Their blood uses copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-based hemoglobin, which makes it blue.

title: Bananas are slightly radioactive
summary: Bananas are rich in potassium, and a small fraction of natural potassium is the radioactive isotope potassium-40. The dose is tiny and harmless, but it is measurable.

title: Sharks are older than trees
summary: The earliest shark-like fish appear in the fossil record around 450 million years ago. The first true trees, like Archaeopteris, appeared roughly 385 million years ago.

title: Wombats poop cubes
summary: Wombats are the only known animals that produce cube-shaped droppings. A 2021 study found that varying stiffness in the walls of their intestines shapes the faeces into cubes.

title: The sunlight you see is 8 minutes old
summary: Light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to Earth. If the Sun vanished, you would not notice for over eight minutes.

title: Sunlight takes thousands of years to escape the Sun
summary: Energy made in the Sun's core gets absorbed and re-emitted countless times on its way out. Estimates say it takes tens of thousands of years or more to reach the surface, then only 8 minutes to reach us.

title: Saturn is less dense than water
summary: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 grams per cubic centimetre, lower than water's 1.0. In theory, a bathtub big enough would let Saturn float.

title: Over a million Earths fit inside the Sun
summary: The Sun's volume is roughly 1.3 million times that of Earth. It holds about 99.8 percent of all the mass in the solar system.

title: Footprints on the Moon could last millions of years
summary: The Moon has no wind or water to erode the ground. Apollo astronauts' footprints are only slowly worn down by tiny meteorite impacts and could survive for millions of years.

title: The mantis shrimp punches like a bullet
summary: The peacock mantis shrimp strikes with a club that accelerates faster than a .22 calibre bullet. The strike is so fast it creates cavitation bubbles that hit prey a second time.

title: Crows remember faces and hold grudges
summary: University of Washington researchers wore masks while trapping crows. Years later, crows still scolded anyone wearing those masks, and even crows that were never trapped learned to do it.

title: Axolotls can regrow limbs, hearts and brains
summary: Axolotls can regenerate entire limbs, parts of their heart, spinal cord and even brain without scarring. Scientists study them to understand regeneration in humans.

title: The jellyfish that can reverse its ageing
summary: Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into its juvenile polyp stage when stressed or injured. In principle this cycle can repeat indefinitely, earning it the nickname 'immortal jellyfish'.

title: Ocean plankton make about half our oxygen
summary: Phytoplankton in the ocean produce roughly half of the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere through photosynthesis. Every other breath you take comes from the sea.

title: Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
summary: A lightning bolt can heat the air to around 30,000 kelvin. That is about five times hotter than the visible surface of the Sun.

title: Water can boil and freeze at the same time
summary: At the triple point, a specific low pressure and temperature, water exists as solid, liquid and gas at once. In a vacuum chamber you can watch it boil and freeze simultaneously.

title: Mars has a volcano nearly three times taller than Everest
summary: Olympus Mons on Mars rises about 22 kilometres high, roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest. Its base is about the size of Poland.

title: A planet where it rains glass sideways
summary: NASA says the exoplanet HD 189733b likely has silicate particles in its atmosphere. With winds around 7,000 km/h, it may rain glass sideways.

title: Astronauts grow taller in space
summary: Without gravity compressing the spine, astronauts can grow up to about 3 percent taller in orbit. They shrink back after returning to Earth.

title: You are about half bacteria — not 90 percent
summary: The popular claim that bacteria outnumber your cells 10 to 1 is a myth. A 2016 estimate found the ratio is closer to 1 to 1.

title: Your body glows in the dark
summary: A 2009 Japanese study using ultra-sensitive cameras found that human bodies emit visible light. The glow is about 1,000 times too weak for our eyes to see.

title: Your cornea breathes air directly
summary: The cornea has no blood vessels so it can stay transparent. It gets most of its oxygen dissolved directly from the air.

title: Koala fingerprints look human
summary: Koalas have fingerprints so similar to human ones that even under a microscope they are very hard to tell apart.

title: A hummingbird's heart beats over 1,200 times a minute
summary: Hummingbirds have the fastest metabolism of any warm-blooded animal. Their hearts can beat more than 1,200 times per minute during flight.

title: The platypus glows under UV light
summary: In 2020 scientists found that platypus fur glows blue-green under ultraviolet light. The platypus also lays eggs and males have venomous spurs.

title: A shrimp's snap is as hot as the Sun's surface
summary: The pistol shrimp snaps its claw so fast it creates a collapsing bubble that briefly reaches about 4,700 degrees Celsius and emits a flash of light.

title: Elephants hear through their feet
summary: Elephants can detect low-frequency rumbles travelling through the ground. Sensitive receptors in their feet let them sense signals from other elephants kilometres away.

title: Dolphins call each other by name
summary: Bottlenose dolphins develop unique signature whistles. Research shows they respond when they hear their own whistle copied, much like a name.

title: Venus is hotter than Mercury
summary: Mercury is closer to the Sun, but Venus is the hottest planet. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping its surface around 465 degrees Celsius.

title: Uranus spins on its side
summary: Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees, so it essentially rolls around the Sun on its side. Each pole gets around 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.

title: A teaspoon of soil holds billions of microbes
summary: A single teaspoon of healthy soil can contain more microorganisms than there are people on Earth.

title: Glass frogs hide their blood to turn invisible
summary: A 2022 study found that sleeping glass frogs pack most of their red blood cells into their liver. This makes their bodies two to three times more transparent.

title: Honeybees understand the concept of zero
summary: A 2018 study showed honeybees can learn that an empty set is 'less than' one. Zero was once thought to be understood only by humans and a few primates.

title: Rats laugh when you tickle them
summary: Neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp found that rats make ultrasonic chirps when tickled. They seek out the hand that tickles them, suggesting they enjoy it.

title: The Greenland shark can live for centuries
summary: Radiocarbon dating of their eye lenses suggests Greenland sharks can live at least 272 years and possibly over 400, making them the longest-lived vertebrates known.

title: Earth's core is as hot as the Sun's surface
summary: Earth's inner core is estimated at around 5,200 degrees Celsius, similar to the surface of the Sun. It stays solid because of the enormous pressure.

title: It may rain diamonds on Neptune and Uranus
summary: Laboratory experiments suggest that deep inside Neptune and Uranus, extreme pressure can squeeze carbon into diamonds that sink toward the core.

title: Cold water on your face slows your heart
summary: The mammalian dive reflex kicks in when your face hits cold water. Your heart rate slows and blood shifts to your vital organs to conserve oxygen.

title: Antarctica is the world's largest desert
summary: A desert is defined by low precipitation, not heat. Antarctica receives so little snow and rain that it is the largest desert on Earth.

title: Everest isn't the tallest mountain
summary: Everest has the highest peak above sea level. Measured from base to summit, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is taller at over 10,000 metres, most of it underwater.

title: Strawberries aren't berries but bananas are
summary: Botanically, a berry develops from a single flower with one ovary. Bananas, grapes and even avocados qualify; strawberries and raspberries do not.

title: The gold in your jewellery came from colliding stars
summary: Much of the universe's gold is forged when neutron stars collide. In 2017 astronomers watched such a collision and detected signs of heavy elements being created.

title: You're taller in the morning
summary: During the day, gravity compresses the discs in your spine. Most people are about a centimetre taller when they wake up than when they go to bed.

title: Male seahorses give birth
summary: Female seahorses deposit eggs into a pouch on the male. He fertilises and carries them, then gives birth to hundreds of babies.

title: Octopus arms have minds of their own
summary: About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, not its brain. Each arm can taste, touch and react on its own.

title: Butterflies taste with their feet
summary: Butterflies have taste receptors on their feet. Females 'taste' leaves by standing on them to find the right plant to lay eggs on.

title: The Moon is drifting away from Earth
summary: Laser measurements show the Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres farther from Earth every year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

title: Days were shorter when dinosaurs lived
summary: Earth's rotation is gradually slowing. A 2020 study of a fossil shell suggests that about 70 million years ago a day lasted about 23.5 hours and a year had about 372 days.

title: Your brain uses 20 percent of your energy
summary: The brain is only about 2 percent of your body weight but consumes roughly 20 percent of its energy at rest.

title: Honey found in ancient tombs is still edible
summary: Honey's low moisture and acidity stop bacteria from growing. Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that had not spoiled.

title: Sloths can hold their breath for 40 minutes
summary: Sloths can slow their heart rate dramatically, letting them hold their breath for up to 40 minutes underwater. They are surprisingly good swimmers.

title: Your stomach acid can dissolve metal
summary: Stomach acid has a pH of around 1.5 to 3.5, strong enough to dissolve some metals like zinc. Your stomach protects itself with a constantly renewed layer of mucus.

title: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids
summary: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, closer in time to the 1969 Moon landing than to the pyramid's construction.

title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire
summary: Teaching at Oxford existed by 1096. The Aztec city of Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.

title: Napoleon wasn't actually short
summary: Napoleon was about 5 feet 7 inches, average for his time. The myth came from confusion between French and British inches and British cartoons.

title: Vikings never wore horned helmets
summary: No horned Viking battle helmet has ever been found. The image was popularised by costume designs for Wagner's operas in the 1870s.

title: Australia lost a war against emus
summary: In 1932 the Australian military used machine guns to cull emus damaging crops in Western Australia. The emus proved so hard to hit that the operation was largely a failure.

title: The dancing plague of 1518
summary: In July 1518 in Strasbourg, a woman began dancing in the street and could not stop. Within weeks dozens more joined, dancing for days in a mysterious mass hysteria.

title: The shortest war lasted under an hour
summary: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted roughly 38 to 45 minutes before Zanzibar surrendered. It is considered the shortest war in recorded history.

title: Woolly mammoths lived while the pyramids were built
summary: A small population of woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, centuries after the Great Pyramid was completed.

title: Ancient Romans taxed urine
summary: Romans collected urine for washing clothes and tanning leather. Emperor Vespasian taxed it, giving rise to the saying 'pecunia non olet' — money doesn't stink.

title: Russia arrived 12 days late to the 1908 Olympics
summary: Russia still used the Julian calendar in 1908, which was 13 days behind the Gregorian one. Its shooting team reportedly showed up in London after the event.

title: Ketchup was once sold as medicine
summary: In the 1830s an American physician promoted tomato ketchup as a cure for indigestion, and it was sold in pill form.

title: The lighter was invented before the match
summary: Johann Döbereiner created a hydrogen lighter in 1823. The friction match was invented by John Walker in 1826.

title: The fax machine is older than the telephone
summary: Alexander Bain patented an early fax-like device in 1843. Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876.

title: The Great Fire of London barely killed anyone
summary: The 1666 fire destroyed over 13,000 houses and St Paul's Cathedral. Yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded.

title: Medieval people knew the Earth was round
summary: Educated people in the Middle Ages widely accepted that the Earth was a sphere. The 'flat Earth' belief was largely invented by 19th-century writers.

title: Tug of war was an Olympic sport
summary: Tug of war was part of the Summer Olympics from 1900 to 1920. Britain won the most medals.

title: Boston's deadly molasses flood
summary: In 1919 a giant tank burst in Boston, releasing a wave of molasses that swept through streets at about 35 mph. It killed 21 people.

title: The pyramids weren't built by slaves
summary: Tombs of pyramid workers found near Giza show they were paid labourers who were fed well and buried with honour near the pharaoh.

title: Ancient Egypt's pregnancy test actually worked
summary: An ancient Egyptian test had women urinate on wheat and barley seeds. A 1963 experiment found that the urine of pregnant women did make the seeds sprout about 70 percent of the time.

title: Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants
summary: In 218 BC Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army with war elephants across the Alps to invade Rome.

title: Roman concrete heals its own cracks
summary: A 2023 MIT study found that lime chunks in Roman concrete react with water seeping into cracks, forming new minerals that seal them. That's why Roman structures still stand.

title: A 2,000-year-old computer found in a shipwreck
summary: The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a Greek shipwreck, used dozens of bronze gears to predict eclipses and planetary positions. It is often called the first analogue computer.

title: Tutankhamun's dagger came from space
summary: A 2016 analysis showed the iron blade of a dagger buried with Tutankhamun was made from meteorite iron.

title: Coca-Cola once contained cocaine
summary: When Coca-Cola launched in 1886, it contained an extract of coca leaves. Cocaine was removed from the recipe in the early 1900s.

title: The Eiffel Tower was supposed to be temporary
summary: The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair with a 20-year permit. It was saved from demolition because it was useful as a radio antenna.

title: The Statue of Liberty used to be brown
summary: The Statue of Liberty is covered in copper and was originally a shiny brown. Over about 20 years, oxidation turned it the green we know.

title: Carrots weren't always orange
summary: Early cultivated carrots were mostly purple or yellow. Orange carrots became widespread after Dutch growers developed them in the 17th century.

title: Abraham Lincoln is in the Wrestling Hall of Fame
summary: As a young man Lincoln was an accomplished wrestler, losing only one recorded match. He was honoured by the National Wrestling Hall of Fame.

title: Einstein was offered the presidency of Israel
summary: In 1952 Israel's prime minister offered Albert Einstein the presidency. Einstein declined, saying he lacked the aptitude for dealing with people.

title: Ancient Romans had fast food
summary: Pompeii had dozens of thermopolia — street counters serving hot food and drinks. One excavated in 2020 still had painted menus and food residue.

title: London's Great Stink built modern sewers
summary: In the hot summer of 1858 the smell of sewage in the Thames was so bad Parliament acted fast. Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system that followed still serves London.

title: Nintendo was founded in 1889
summary: Nintendo began in Kyoto in 1889 making hanafuda playing cards. It tried taxis and love hotels before moving into video games.

title: A volcano caused a year without summer
summary: Mount Tambora's 1815 eruption cooled the planet, causing snow in June in parts of the US and crop failures in Europe. Stuck indoors that summer, Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein.

title: The first computer bug was a real moth
summary: In 1947 engineers working on the Harvard Mark II found a moth trapped in a relay. They taped it in the logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found'.

title: Apollo 11's computer had less memory than a calculator
summary: The Apollo Guidance Computer had about 4 KB of erasable memory and 72 KB of read-only memory. A modern smartphone has millions of times more.

title: The first webcam watched a coffee pot
summary: In 1991 Cambridge University researchers pointed a camera at their coffee pot so they could check if it was full. It later went online and became the first webcam.

title: Why the @ symbol is in every email
summary: In 1971 Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email and chose the @ sign to separate the user from the computer name.

title: The first YouTube video was 19 seconds at a zoo
summary: YouTube's first video, 'Me at the zoo', was uploaded in April 2005 by co-founder Jawed Karim. It is 19 seconds of him in front of elephants.

title: Wi-Fi came from hunting exploding black holes
summary: Australian radio astronomers at CSIRO developed techniques to detect signals from evaporating black holes. That work led to a key patent behind modern Wi-Fi.

title: The microwave was invented by a melted chocolate bar
summary: In 1945 engineer Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar in his pocket melted while he worked near radar equipment. That led to the first microwave oven.

title: More chess games exist than atoms in the universe
summary: Claude Shannon estimated around 10^120 possible chess games. The observable universe contains roughly 10^80 atoms.

title: GPS only works because of Einstein
summary: Clocks on GPS satellites run about 38 microseconds a day faster than on Earth because of relativity. Without correcting for it, GPS positions would drift by kilometres every day.

title: A Hollywood star co-invented the tech behind Wi-Fi
summary: Actress Hedy Lamarr co-invented a frequency-hopping system in 1942 to stop torpedoes being jammed. Similar spread-spectrum ideas are used in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

title: Velcro was copied from burrs on a dog
summary: In 1941 Swiss engineer George de Mestral noticed burrs stuck to his dog's fur. Studying their tiny hooks under a microscope led him to invent Velcro.

title: Someone paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas
summary: On 22 May 2010 a programmer paid 10,000 bitcoin for two Papa John's pizzas, the first known real-world bitcoin purchase. Those coins later became worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

title: The internet runs on cables under the ocean
summary: About 99 percent of intercontinental data travels through undersea fibre-optic cables, not satellites.

title: You trained AI every time you solved a CAPTCHA
summary: Google's reCAPTCHA used people's answers to digitise old books and newspapers, and later to label images that helped train machine learning systems.

title: Voyager 1 is still talking to us from interstellar space
summary: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object. Its signals take almost a full day to reach Earth, yet it still sends data.

title: The first text message said Merry Christmas
summary: On 3 December 1992 engineer Neil Papworth sent 'Merry Christmas' from a computer to a mobile phone. It was the first SMS.

title: Mario has a moustache because of pixels
summary: Shigeru Miyamoto gave Mario a moustache and cap because early hardware had too few pixels to draw a mouth and hair clearly.

title: NASA didn't spend millions on a space pen
summary: The story that NASA spent millions on a space pen while Russia used pencils is a myth. The Fisher pen was privately developed, and both agencies bought it.

title: The first 1 GB hard drive weighed 250 kg
summary: IBM's 3380 in 1980 was the first drive to store a gigabyte. It was the size of a refrigerator and cost tens of thousands of dollars.

title: A bird redesigned Japan's bullet train
summary: Early Shinkansen trains made loud booms exiting tunnels. Engineer Eiji Nakatsu reshaped the nose after a kingfisher's beak, making it quieter and more efficient.

title: We still bounce lasers off mirrors on the Moon
summary: Apollo astronauts left retroreflectors on the Moon. Observatories still fire lasers at them to measure the Earth-Moon distance to within millimetres.

title: Apollo 13 was saved with duct tape
summary: When carbon dioxide built up in Apollo 13's lunar module, engineers improvised a fix using duct tape, plastic bags and cardboard to fit square filters into round sockets.

title: Why you can't tickle yourself
summary: Your cerebellum predicts the sensations caused by your own movements and dampens them. Without surprise, the tickle doesn't work.

title: The Baader-Meinhof phenomenon
summary: After learning something new, you suddenly notice it everywhere. This frequency illusion is selective attention plus confirmation bias.

title: Doorways make you forget
summary: Studies by Gabriel Radvansky found that walking through a doorway makes people more likely to forget what they were doing. The brain treats it as an event boundary.

title: Your brain hides a hole in your vision
summary: Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve connects and there are no light receptors. Your brain fills it in so you never notice.

title: The man with an iron rod through his brain
summary: In 1848 Phineas Gage survived an iron rod blasting through his skull. Reports of his personality change shaped early understanding of the frontal lobe.

title: The invisible gorilla
summary: In a famous 1999 study, about half of people counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene.

title: The Mandela effect
summary: Many people vividly remember 'The Berenstein Bears', but it was always 'Berenstain'. Shared false memories show how memory reconstructs rather than records.

title: Placebos work even when you know they're fake
summary: In a 2010 Harvard study, patients with irritable bowel syndrome improved after taking pills they were openly told were placebos.

title: Why the first second on a clock lasts longer
summary: When you glance at a clock, the second hand seems to freeze. Your brain backfills the moment your eyes were moving — an illusion called chronostasis.

title: Your eyes can change what you hear
summary: In the McGurk effect, watching lips say 'ga' while hearing 'ba' makes most people hear 'da'. Vision overrides sound.

title: Ask a favour to make someone like you
summary: The Ben Franklin effect: people tend to like you more after doing you a favour, because they justify their own behaviour.

title: Why smells trigger the strongest memories
summary: Smell signals go directly to brain areas tied to emotion and memory, the amygdala and hippocampus. That's why a scent can instantly bring back a childhood moment.

title: Nobody notices you as much as you think
summary: In the spotlight effect study, students wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed half the room noticed. Only about a quarter did.

title: Why you see faces in everything
summary: Pareidolia makes us see faces in clouds, plugs and toast. Our brains evolved to detect faces quickly, even when they aren't there.

title: Every time you remember, you rewrite the memory
summary: Memories become unstable when recalled and are stored again afterwards. This reconsolidation means memories can change slightly every time you remember them.

title: The Tetris effect
summary: After playing Tetris for hours, people report seeing falling blocks when they close their eyes. Repeated activities can shape your thoughts and dreams.

title: The woman who survived the Titanic and its sister ships
summary: Violet Jessop was aboard the Olympic when it collided with a warship in 1911, survived the Titanic in 1912, and survived the Britannic sinking in 1916.

title: The man who survived both atomic bombs
summary: Tsutomu Yamaguchi was in Hiroshima on business when the bomb fell. He returned home to Nagasaki and survived the second bomb three days later.

title: The soldier who fought WWII until 1974
summary: Japanese officer Hiroo Onoda kept fighting in the Philippine jungle for 29 years, refusing to believe the war had ended until his former commander came to relieve him.

title: The man struck by lightning seven times
summary: US park ranger Roy Sullivan was struck by lightning seven times between 1942 and 1977 and survived every one.

title: The girl who fell 3 km and walked out of the jungle
summary: In 1971 17-year-old Juliane Koepcke fell from a plane broken up by lightning over the Amazon. She survived the fall and walked for 11 days to find help.

title: The con man who sold the Eiffel Tower
summary: In 1925 Victor Lustig posed as a government official and convinced a scrap dealer to buy the Eiffel Tower. He reportedly tried it a second time.

title: Typhoid Mary
summary: Mary Mallon, a cook in New York, carried typhoid without symptoms and infected dozens of people. She was forcibly quarantined for nearly 30 years.

title: The pirate queen who beat three navies
summary: Ching Shih commanded a pirate fleet of hundreds of ships in early 19th-century China. She negotiated a pardon and retired with her fortune.

title: The man who stopped a nuclear war
summary: In 1983 Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov saw alerts of incoming US missiles. He judged it a false alarm and didn't report it up the chain. He was right.

title: Hachiko, the dog who waited nine years
summary: After his owner died in 1925, the Akita dog Hachiko returned to Shibuya Station every day for about nine years to wait for him.

title: The bear who joined the army
summary: Wojtek, a Syrian brown bear, was adopted by Polish soldiers in WWII. He was enlisted as a private and reportedly helped carry ammunition.

title: Shackleton's impossible rescue
summary: After his ship Endurance was crushed by Antarctic ice in 1915, Ernest Shackleton led a rescue across the ocean in a lifeboat. Every crew member survived. The wreck was found in 2022.

title: The hijacker who vanished
summary: In 1971 a man known as D. B. Cooper hijacked a plane, collected a $200,000 ransom and parachuted into the night. He was never identified.

title: The mystery of Dyatlov Pass
summary: In 1959 nine hikers died in the Ural Mountains after cutting their way out of their tent. In 2020 scientists showed a small slab avalanche could explain it.

title: Mike the headless chicken
summary: In 1945 a Colorado farmer's chicken survived having its head cut off because enough brain stem remained. Mike lived for 18 months.

title: Sherlock Holmes' creator believed in fairies
summary: In 1917 two English girls photographed 'fairies' in Cottingley. Arthur Conan Doyle championed the photos. The girls admitted in the 1980s they used paper cut-outs.

title: The real Robinson Crusoe
summary: Sailor Alexander Selkirk was marooned on a Pacific island for over four years from 1704. His story is thought to have inspired Robinson Crusoe.

title: The woman who claimed to be a lost princess
summary: Anna Anderson claimed for decades to be Grand Duchess Anastasia, who survived the Romanov execution. DNA tests after her death proved she was not.
